lesson_title: Why a Rupee Today Beats a Rupee Tomorrow
question_or_heading: Money today can start earning immediately
option_a: ₹1,000 in your hand right now can be deposited, invested, or lent out today — and start growing. ₹1,000 promised a year from now has none of that earning time.

lesson_title: Why a Rupee Today Beats a Rupee Tomorrow
question_or_heading: Inflation and risk make it worse
option_a: A future rupee also buys less (inflation) and isn't fully guaranteed (risk of non-payment). Both push its value further below a rupee in hand today.

lesson_title: Why a Rupee Today Beats a Rupee Tomorrow
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: The time value of money: a rupee available today is worth more than a rupee available later, because of its earning potential, inflation, and risk.

lesson_title: Why a Rupee Today Beats a Rupee Tomorrow
question_or_heading: Why is ₹10,000 today worth more than a guaranteed ₹10,000 in exactly one year?
option_a: Because rupees physically wear out over time
option_b: Because today's ₹10,000 can be invested and start earning for a full year that the future amount misses
option_c: Because banks refuse to accept old currency
option_d: There's no real difference between the two
hint: What can you do with money today that you can't do with a future promise?
explanation: Today's money has a full year of earning potential ahead of it that the future amount simply doesn't get.

lesson_title: Why a Rupee Today Beats a Rupee Tomorrow
question_or_heading: Which of these is NOT a standard reason a future rupee is worth less than a present one?
option_a: Lost earning/investment time
option_b: Inflation eroding purchasing power
option_c: Risk that the payment might not actually happen
option_d: The number '10,000' looks smaller when written in the future
hint: Which option is just nonsense dressed up as an economic reason?
explanation: Three real forces reduce a future rupee's value: lost earning time, inflation, and payment risk. The fourth option isn't a real financial concept.

lesson_title: Why a Rupee Today Beats a Rupee Tomorrow
question_or_heading: If there were zero inflation and zero risk of non-payment, the time value of money would completely disappear.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Even with zero inflation and zero risk, is there still an opportunity to invest money starting today?
explanation: Even without inflation or risk, money today can still be invested and start earning — so today's rupee remains worth more purely from that earning-time advantage.

lesson_title: Why a Rupee Today Beats a Rupee Tomorrow
question_or_heading: A friend offers you ₹5,000 today or ₹5,000 in exactly two years, guaranteed with zero risk. Assuming you have any use for money now, which should you prefer, and why?
option_a: ₹5,000 in two years, since it feels safer
option_b: ₹5,000 today, since it can be invested and grow before the two years are up
option_c: Both are exactly equal, always
option_d: Neither — you should refuse both
hint: Which option gives you more time to put the money to work?
explanation: With equal amounts and zero risk, today's money is still preferable purely because of the two extra years it has to earn a return.

lesson_title: Why a Rupee Today Beats a Rupee Tomorrow
question_or_heading: A country experiencing high inflation makes the time value of money:
option_a: Irrelevant, since prices are unstable anyway
option_b: Even more pronounced, since future rupees lose purchasing power faster
option_c: Reversed, so future money becomes more valuable
option_d: Impossible to calculate
hint: What does high inflation do to the purchasing power of money you'll receive later?
explanation: Higher inflation erodes a future rupee's purchasing power faster, making the gap between present and future value even wider.

question_or_heading: Simple interest: only the original amount earns
option_a: With simple interest, you earn a return only on your starting principal, every period, regardless of how much interest has already piled up.

question_or_heading: Compound interest: interest earns interest too
option_a: With compounding, each period's interest gets added to your balance, and the next period earns a return on that larger amount — growth accelerates the longer it runs.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Compounding means earning returns not just on your original money, but on the returns it has already generated.

question_or_heading: ₹10,000 invested at 10% simple interest for 3 years earns interest of:
option_a: ₹1,000 total
option_b: ₹3,000 total, since it's 10% of ₹10,000 every year
option_c: ₹3,310, compounding each year
option_d: ₹10,000 total
hint: With simple interest, does the interest base ever change?
explanation: Simple interest always applies to the same original ₹10,000, so it's 10% × 3 years = ₹3,000 flat, with no acceleration.

question_or_heading: ₹10,000 invested at 10% compound interest, compounded annually for 3 years, grows to approximately:
hint: Each year's interest gets added before the next year's 10% is calculated — try it year by year.
explanation: Year 1: ₹11,000. Year 2: ₹12,100. Year 3: ₹13,310 — each year's 10% applies to a growing balance, not just the original ₹10,000.

question_or_heading: Over a long enough time horizon, compound interest will always produce a larger balance than simple interest at the same rate.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does compounding's advantage shrink or grow the longer the money is left to grow?
explanation: Compounding's edge over simple interest grows larger the longer the money compounds — the gap widens every additional period.

question_or_heading: Which savings product would you expect to grow your money faster over 20 years, all else equal?
option_a: One paying 6% simple interest
option_b: One paying 6% interest compounded annually
option_c: They'll always be identical
option_d: It depends only on the currency used
hint: Which one lets interest itself start earning more interest?
explanation: Compounding lets each year's interest join the base that earns future interest — over 20 years that produces meaningfully more growth than simple interest at the same rate.

question_or_heading: Why do lenders and investors generally care so much about whether interest compounds annually, monthly, or daily?
option_a: It makes no real difference to the final amount
option_b: More frequent compounding means interest gets added to the base more often, slightly increasing total growth for the same stated rate
option_c: Daily compounding is illegal in most countries
option_d: Compounding frequency only matters for loans, never for investments
hint: What happens to the base that earns interest as compounding frequency increases?
explanation: More frequent compounding means interest gets folded into the principal more often, which — for the same annual rate — produces a slightly higher effective return.

question_or_heading: Future value answers: what will this grow to?
option_a: Future value (FV) takes an amount today and projects what it becomes after earning a given rate of return for a number of periods.

question_or_heading: The formula, plainly
option_a: FV = Present Value × (1 + rate) raised to the power of the number of periods. The rate and the number of periods must use the same time unit — both annual, or both monthly.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Future value = Present Value × (1 + rate)^periods — money grows by compounding over time.

question_or_heading: ₹1,00,000 invested for 2 years at 8% annual compound interest has a future value closest to:
hint: Calculate year by year: ₹1,00,000 × 1.08, then that result × 1.08 again.
explanation: ₹1,00,000 × 1.08 = ₹1,08,000 after year 1; × 1.08 again = ₹1,16,640 after year 2 — that's compounding, not simple 16% flat.

question_or_heading: If you double the number of years money compounds at a positive rate, does the future value simply double too?
option_a: Yes, always exactly double
option_b: No — because of compounding, it typically grows by more than double
option_c: No — it grows by exactly the same amount added twice
option_d: Future value only depends on the rate, never the time
hint: Does compounding produce straight-line growth or accelerating growth?
explanation: Because interest earns interest, doubling the time period usually more than doubles the future value — growth accelerates, it doesn't stay linear.

question_or_heading: A higher assumed interest rate, holding time constant, always produces a higher future value.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does a bigger rate multiplier each period lead to a smaller or larger ending balance?
explanation: A higher rate compounds more aggressively each period, so — holding time fixed — future value rises as the assumed rate rises.

question_or_heading: Which of these would produce the LARGEST future value for the same starting amount?
option_a: 5% for 5 years
option_b: 5% for 10 years
option_c: 10% for 10 years
option_d: 10% for 5 years
hint: Compare both a higher rate and more time against the alternatives.
explanation: Both a higher rate and more time increase future value — combining the highest rate (10%) with the longest time (10 years) beats every other combination here.

question_or_heading: Why does the future-value formula raise (1 + rate) to the power of the number of periods, rather than just multiplying by the number of periods?
option_a: It's a typo that persists in finance textbooks
option_b: Because compounding means each period's growth builds on all prior growth, which multiplication (not addition) captures
option_c: Because interest rates are always expressed as percentages
option_d: Powers are only used for very long time horizons
hint: Which mathematical operation captures growth building on prior growth — repeated addition, or repeated multiplication?
explanation: Raising to a power captures repeated multiplication — each period's balance is multiplied by (1+rate) again, which is exactly what compounding means mechanically.

question_or_heading: Present value runs the clock backward
option_a: Present value (PV) asks the reverse question: given a future amount, what is it worth today, after 'shrinking' it by the discount rate for however many periods stand between now and then?

question_or_heading: The formula, plainly
option_a: PV = Future Value ÷ (1 + rate) raised to the power of the number of periods. A higher rate, or more periods, shrinks the present value further.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Present value = Future Value ÷ (1 + rate)^periods — it tells you what a future rupee is worth in today's terms.

question_or_heading: What is the present value of ₹1,21,000 to be received in exactly 2 years, using a 10% discount rate?
hint: Divide by 1.10 twice, once for each year.
explanation: ₹1,21,000 ÷ 1.10 = ₹1,10,000 after undoing one year; ÷ 1.10 again = ₹1,00,000 — the present value of that future amount.

question_or_heading: Holding the future amount and discount rate constant, what happens to present value as the number of years until payment increases?
option_a: Present value increases
option_b: Present value decreases
option_c: Present value stays exactly the same
option_d: Present value becomes negative
hint: Are you discounting for more periods or fewer as the wait gets longer?
explanation: More years of discounting shrinks the present value further — money further in the future is worth less today.

question_or_heading: A higher discount rate results in a higher present value for the same future cash flow.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Think about what a bigger divisor does to a fraction.
explanation: A higher discount rate is a bigger divisor at each period, which shrinks — not grows — the present value of a given future amount.

question_or_heading: Two investors value the same ₹10,00,000 payment due in 5 years, but Investor A uses a 6% discount rate and Investor B uses a 12% discount rate. Whose present value estimate will be lower?
option_a: Investor A's
option_b: Investor B's
option_c: They'll be identical
option_d: It depends on the currency
hint: Which discount rate shrinks future money more aggressively?
explanation: A higher discount rate (12% vs 6%) discounts the future payment more heavily, producing a lower present value estimate for Investor B.

question_or_heading: Why might an investor deliberately use a HIGHER discount rate when valuing an uncertain or risky future cash flow?
option_a: Higher rates are only used for guaranteed, risk-free payments
option_b: A higher discount rate compensates for extra risk by shrinking the present value of an uncertain payment more aggressively
option_c: Discount rates have nothing to do with risk
option_d: It's simply a rounding convention with no real meaning
hint: How should extra uncertainty about actually receiving that future cash flow affect how much you're willing to pay for it today?
explanation: A higher discount rate is a common way to build in a risk cushion — it makes an uncertain future payment worth less today than an equally-sized guaranteed one.

question_or_heading: A discount rate is your required return
option_a: The discount rate represents the minimum annual return you'd need to be willing to wait for that future money instead of having it now — it reflects both opportunity cost and risk.

question_or_heading: Riskier cash flows deserve higher discount rates
option_a: A guaranteed government payment might use a low discount rate. A speculative startup's projected cash flow deserves a much higher one, because there's more that could go wrong.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: The discount rate is the return you require to compensate for waiting and for the risk that the future payment might not arrive as expected.

question_or_heading: Which investment would typically be discounted using a LOWER discount rate?
option_a: A pre-revenue startup's projected cash flows
option_b: A government bond's promised interest payments
option_c: A speculative mining exploration project
option_d: A brand-new company with no track record
hint: Which of these carries the least uncertainty about actually receiving the payment?
explanation: Government bond payments are about as close to guaranteed as cash flows get, which justifies discounting them at a comparatively low rate.

question_or_heading: A venture capital investor discounting a risky startup's projected future cash flows at 30%, versus a bank discounting a safe corporate loan's payments at 6%, mainly reflects a difference in:
option_a: The currency being used
option_b: The perceived risk and uncertainty of each cash flow actually materializing
option_c: A typo in one of the calculations
option_d: The length of time involved, which is unrelated to risk
hint: What's driving such a large gap between the two rates?
explanation: The huge gap in discount rates mirrors a huge gap in how confident each party can be that the projected cash flow will actually show up.

question_or_heading: The discount rate you choose has no real effect on how much you'd be willing to pay today for a future cash flow.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Recall from the last lesson: what does a higher discount rate do to present value?
explanation: The discount rate directly shrinks or expands present value — choosing it carelessly can make a valuation wildly too optimistic or too conservative.

question_or_heading: An analyst uses the same low discount rate to value both a stable utility company's cash flows and a speculative biotech's cash flows. What's the most likely problem with this approach?
option_a: There's no problem — one discount rate always fits every company
option_b: It probably overvalues the riskier biotech, since its higher uncertainty isn't being reflected in the discount rate
option_c: It definitely undervalues both companies
option_d: Discount rates should never differ by company, only by country
hint: Which company's true risk is not being captured by a single low rate?
explanation: Using the same low rate for a much riskier cash flow understates how much that extra risk should shrink its present value — producing an inflated valuation for the biotech.

question_or_heading: Why is the choice of discount rate often described as one of the most consequential assumptions in a valuation?
option_a: Because it has almost no effect on the final number
option_b: Because even small changes in the discount rate can meaningfully swing the present value of far-future cash flows
option_c: Because regulators fix the discount rate by law
option_d: Because it's the only assumption anyone ever double-checks
hint: Recall how compounding (and its mirror, discounting) accelerates over many periods — what does that imply about small rate changes?
explanation: Because discounting compounds over many periods, even a small change in the rate can meaningfully swing the present value of cash flows far in the future.

question_or_heading: An annuity is a series of equal, regular payments
option_a: A fixed monthly loan EMI, a regular pension payout, or level rental income are all annuities — the same amount, paid at regular intervals, for a set number of periods.

question_or_heading: Valuing an annuity is just valuing many single payments, added up
option_a: Technically, the present value of an annuity is the sum of the present values of each individual payment — but there's a shortcut formula that does this in one step.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: An annuity is a stream of equal payments at regular intervals; its present value discounts every payment back to today and adds them together.

question_or_heading: A loan that requires you to pay exactly ₹20,000 every month for 3 years is an example of:
option_a: A perpetuity
option_b: An annuity
option_c: A single lump-sum payment
option_d: A dividend
hint: Are the payments equal, regular, and for a fixed number of periods?
explanation: Equal payments at regular intervals for a defined number of periods is the textbook definition of an annuity.

question_or_heading: Which of these is the correct way to think about valuing a 5-year annuity?
option_a: Just look at the final payment and ignore the rest
option_b: Discount each of the 5 payments back to today individually, then add them up (or use the annuity shortcut formula for the same result)
option_c: Multiply the payment amount by the interest rate only
option_d: Annuities can't be valued using time value of money at all
hint: What's the relationship between an annuity's value and the value of its individual payments?
explanation: An annuity's present value is simply the sum of the present values of all its individual payments — the annuity formula is just a faster way to get there.

question_or_heading: All else equal, an annuity paying the same total amount but spread over MORE payments (say, monthly instead of annually) will have a slightly higher present value.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Which pays you sooner, on average — monthly installments or fewer, larger annual ones for the same total?
explanation: More frequent payments mean you receive money sooner on average, which — thanks to the time value of money — nudges present value slightly higher for the same total nominal amount.

question_or_heading: A retiree is choosing between a lump sum of ₹50,00,000 today, or an annuity of ₹5,00,000 per year for 15 years. What's the right way to compare these options?
option_a: Just add up the annuity payments (₹75,00,000) and compare that to ₹50,00,000
option_b: Compute the present value of the annuity using an appropriate discount rate, then compare that to the ₹50,00,000 lump sum
option_c: Always take the annuity, since the total is bigger
option_d: Always take the lump sum, since it's paid immediately
hint: Can you fairly compare money spread over 15 years to money today without discounting?
explanation: Comparing raw totals ignores the time value of money entirely — the annuity needs to be discounted to a present value before it's a fair comparison to the lump sum.

question_or_heading: Why do EMIs (equal monthly installments) on a loan stay the same each month, even though the loan balance is shrinking over time?
option_a: EMIs are randomly set and unrelated to the loan balance
option_b: They're structured, using annuity math, so that a fixed payment covers both interest and principal in changing proportions each month
option_c: Interest is only charged in the first month
option_d: Banks are required by law to keep payments flat regardless of the loan
hint: What stays fixed, and what changes, inside each EMI payment over the life of the loan?
explanation: EMI structuring is a direct application of annuity math — the fixed total payment is split differently each month between interest (shrinking) and principal (growing) as the balance declines.

question_or_heading: A perpetuity never ends
option_a: A perpetuity is like an annuity, but the equal payments continue forever, with no final period — some preference shares and certain bonds work this way.

question_or_heading: The perpetuity formula is surprisingly simple
option_a: Present Value of a Perpetuity = Payment ÷ Discount Rate. No time exponent needed — infinity simplifies the math rather than complicating it.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Present value of a perpetuity = annual payment ÷ discount rate — a never-ending stream still has a finite present value.

question_or_heading: A preference share promises to pay ₹80 per year, forever, and investors require a 10% return. What's its approximate present value?
hint: Divide the payment by the discount rate.
explanation: ₹80 ÷ 0.10 = ₹800 — even though the payments never stop, discounting shrinks each future payment enough that the total present value is still finite.

question_or_heading: Why does an infinite stream of payments still have a FINITE present value?
option_a: Because infinite streams are actually a myth
option_b: Because each payment further in the future is discounted so heavily that its present value shrinks toward zero, so the sum still converges
option_c: Because perpetuities are capped by law after 100 years
option_d: Because the discount rate becomes zero after enough time
hint: What happens to the present value of a single payment as it moves further and further into the future?
explanation: Payments far enough in the future get discounted so heavily their present value is nearly nothing — so summing infinitely many of them still adds up to a finite number.

question_or_heading: A higher discount rate results in a lower present value for a perpetuity, just as it does for a single future payment.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Payment ÷ rate — what happens to that fraction as the denominator (rate) grows?
explanation: Since perpetuity value is payment divided by rate, a bigger rate (bigger denominator) produces a smaller present value — the same direction as with any discounting.

question_or_heading: A perpetuity paying ₹1,000 a year is discounted first at 5%, then at 10%. Which discount rate gives the HIGHER present value?
option_c: Both give exactly the same value
option_d: Perpetuities can't be discounted at different rates
hint: Recheck: payment ÷ rate — smaller denominator means what?
explanation: ₹1,000 ÷ 0.05 = ₹20,000, versus ₹1,000 ÷ 0.10 = ₹10,000 — the lower discount rate (5%) produces the higher present value.

question_or_heading: Where does perpetuity math show up in company valuation, even though real companies don't literally pay dividends forever?
option_a: It never shows up in valuation — it's a purely academic idea
option_b: It's often used to estimate 'terminal value' — a simplified stand-in for all the cash flows a business is assumed to generate far into the future
option_c: Only insurance companies use perpetuity formulas
option_d: It's used exclusively for government bonds
hint: Think ahead to how a DCF model handles cash flows beyond its explicit forecast period.
explanation: Perpetuity-style math is the backbone of 'terminal value' in a DCF — a practical way to capture the value of cash flows stretching indefinitely beyond a model's explicit forecast.

question_or_heading: NPV nets the cost against the value it creates
option_a: Net Present Value (NPV) takes all the present values of a project's future cash flows, and subtracts the upfront cost — leaving one number that shows whether the project creates or destroys value.

question_or_heading: The decision rule is simple
option_a: A positive NPV means the project is expected to create more value than it costs — worth doing. A negative NPV means the opposite — walk away.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: NPV = present value of all future cash flows minus the upfront investment — positive NPV means the project is worth undertaking.

question_or_heading: A project costs ₹10,00,000 today and its future cash flows have a present value of ₹13,00,000. What is its NPV, and should it be undertaken?
option_b: NPV = ₹3,00,000; yes, since it's positive
option_d: NPV = ₹13,00,000; maybe
hint: NPV = present value of benefits minus upfront cost.
explanation: ₹13,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 = ₹3,00,000. Since NPV is positive, the project is expected to create more value than it costs — worth doing.

question_or_heading: A project costs ₹5,00,000 and its future cash flows have a present value of only ₹4,20,000. What should a rational decision-maker do?
option_a: Undertake it, since ₹4,20,000 is still a lot of money
option_b: Reject it, since its NPV is negative (-₹80,000), meaning it destroys value
option_c: Undertake it only if the CEO likes the idea
option_d: There's not enough information to decide
hint: Subtract cost from present value of benefits — is the result positive or negative?
explanation: With a negative NPV of -₹80,000, the project is expected to cost more than the value it creates — the standard decision rule says reject it.

question_or_heading: Using a higher discount rate in an NPV calculation makes it easier for a project to show a positive NPV.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: A higher discount rate shrinks the present value of future benefits — does that help or hurt the NPV comparison?
explanation: A higher discount rate shrinks the present value of future cash flows, which tends to pull NPV down, not up — making it harder, not easier, to clear the positive-NPV bar.

question_or_heading: Two projects require the same ₹1,00,00,000 upfront investment. Project A has an NPV of ₹5,00,000; Project B has an NPV of ₹20,00,000. All else equal, which is the better use of that capital?
option_a: Project A, since smaller numbers are safer
option_b: Project B, since it's expected to create significantly more value for the same investment
option_c: They're equally good, since the cost is identical
option_d: Neither — any NPV under ₹1 crore should be rejected
hint: Which project creates more value per rupee invested, based on NPV?
explanation: With identical upfront cost, the project with the higher NPV — Project B — is expected to create meaningfully more value for the same capital outlay.

question_or_heading: Why is NPV generally considered a more complete decision tool than simply looking at a project's total future cash inflows?
option_a: Because NPV ignores the time value of money entirely
option_b: Because NPV both discounts future cash flows to today's terms AND subtracts the upfront cost, capturing both timing and profitability in one number
option_c: Because total future cash inflows are always a better measure
option_d: Because NPV never requires any assumptions
hint: What two things does NPV account for that a simple 'add up all future cash' approach ignores?
explanation: Simply totaling future cash flows ignores both when that cash arrives and what it cost to get it — NPV corrects for both by discounting and netting out the initial investment.

lesson_title: The Rule of 72 & Quick Mental Math
question_or_heading: A shortcut for doubling time
option_a: The Rule of 72 estimates how many years it takes an investment to double at a given annual compound rate: just divide 72 by the interest rate (as a whole number, not a decimal).

lesson_title: The Rule of 72 & Quick Mental Math
question_or_heading: It's an approximation, not exact
option_a: The Rule of 72 is remarkably accurate for rates roughly between 6% and 10%, and gets progressively less precise the further you move from that range — but it's excellent for fast mental estimates.

lesson_title: The Rule of 72 & Quick Mental Math
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual interest rate (as a whole number) — a fast mental shortcut for compounding.

lesson_title: The Rule of 72 & Quick Mental Math
question_or_heading: Using the Rule of 72, roughly how many years will it take an investment to double at 8% annual compound interest?
option_a: 6 years
option_b: 9 years
option_c: 12 years
option_d: 16 years
explanation: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years — a quick, close approximation of how long it'll take that investment to double at an 8% compound rate.

lesson_title: The Rule of 72 & Quick Mental Math
question_or_heading: Using the Rule of 72, an investment growing at 12% per year would roughly double in:
option_a: 4 years
option_b: 6 years
option_c: 10 years
option_d: 24 years
explanation: 72 ÷ 12 = 6 years — at a 12% compound rate, the Rule of 72 estimates your money doubles roughly every 6 years.

lesson_title: The Rule of 72 & Quick Mental Math
question_or_heading: The Rule of 72 gives you a mathematically exact doubling time, not just an estimate.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Re-read the second intro card — how precise is this shortcut described as being?
explanation: It's a close approximation, most accurate for moderate rates — for an exact answer you'd need the full compound growth formula, not this shortcut.

lesson_title: The Rule of 72 & Quick Mental Math
question_or_heading: An investor wants to roughly compare how fast their money would double at 6% versus 9% annual returns, without a calculator. Which tool fits best?
option_a: A full discounted cash flow model
option_b: The Rule of 72
option_c: A balance sheet
option_d: An income statement
hint: Which of the tools listed is specifically built for fast mental doubling-time estimates?
explanation: The Rule of 72 exists exactly for this kind of quick, calculator-free comparison of how fast money grows at different rates.

lesson_title: The Rule of 72 & Quick Mental Math
question_or_heading: Why is the Rule of 72 a genuinely useful skill for someone evaluating investment options quickly, even in the age of calculators and spreadsheets?
option_a: It's more accurate than any spreadsheet formula
option_b: It lets you sanity-check a growth assumption instantly, in your head, without needing any tools at hand
option_c: It's a legal requirement for all financial advisors
option_d: It replaces the need to ever learn compound interest properly
hint: What's the practical value of a fast mental estimate, compared to always needing a tool to check your intuition?
explanation: Being able to instantly sanity-check 'does this growth assumption make sense?' without opening a spreadsheet is exactly the kind of practical intuition the Rule of 72 builds.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Cash Flow Streams
question_or_heading: Every comparison needs a common time reference
option_a: You can never fairly compare ₹1,00,000 today to ₹1,20,000 in three years just by looking at the numbers — they need to be brought to the same point in time first, using a discount rate.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Cash Flow Streams
question_or_heading: Bigger nominal totals don't always win
option_a: A cash flow stream with a larger sum of raw numbers can still be worth less today than a smaller, faster-paid stream — timing matters as much as size.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Cash Flow Streams
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: To compare cash flows fairly, discount every stream to the same point in time using a consistent, appropriately-chosen discount rate.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Cash Flow Streams
question_or_heading: Option A pays ₹1,00,000 today. Option B pays ₹1,15,000 in exactly 2 years. Using a 10% discount rate, which has the higher present value?
option_a: Option A (₹1,00,000 today, already in present value terms)
option_b: Option B, since ₹1,15,000 is a bigger number
option_c: They're exactly equal
option_d: Not enough information to compare them at all
hint: Discount Option B back to today first, then compare like-for-like: ₹1,15,000 ÷ 1.10² ≈ ?
explanation: ₹1,15,000 ÷ (1.10)² ≈ ₹95,041 — that's LESS than Option A's ₹1,00,000, even though ₹1,15,000 looks like the bigger number on paper.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Cash Flow Streams
question_or_heading: Why would a lower nominal amount received sooner sometimes be worth more than a higher nominal amount received later?
option_a: It's never actually true — bigger numbers always win
option_b: Because the earlier amount has more time to earn a return, and the later amount gets discounted more heavily for the extra wait
option_c: Because currency always loses exactly half its value every year
option_d: Because later payments are usually illegal
hint: Which of the two forces — earning time, and discounting for delay — work in favor of the earlier payment?
explanation: Both extra earning time for the early payment and heavier discounting on the delayed one work in the same direction: favoring the sooner cash, if the gap in size isn't big enough to offset it.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Cash Flow Streams
question_or_heading: When comparing two cash flow streams, using two different discount rates for each one (without a specific risk-based reason) would generally be considered fair and standard practice.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Should equally risky, comparable cash flows normally be discounted at different rates just for convenience?
explanation: Unless there's a genuine difference in risk between the two streams, using inconsistent discount rates would distort the comparison — the whole point is applying a fair, consistent basis.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Cash Flow Streams
question_or_heading: An annuity paying ₹2,00,000 a year for 5 years is being compared to a single lump sum of ₹9,00,000 today. What's the correct first step to compare them fairly?
option_a: Just add up the annuity's total (₹10,00,000) and compare that number directly to ₹9,00,000
option_b: Compute the annuity's present value using an appropriate discount rate, and compare that to the ₹9,00,000 lump sum
option_c: Automatically pick whichever option has more payments
option_d: Ignore the lump sum, since it's a single number
hint: What did the earlier annuity lesson say about comparing spread-out payments to a lump sum?
explanation: Just as with the earlier annuity example, you have to discount the spread-out payments to a present value before any fair comparison to a lump sum is possible.

question_or_heading: Pulling together everything from this unit — TVM, compounding, discounting, annuities, perpetuities, NPV, and the Rule of 72 — what's the one idea that connects all of them?
option_a: Money should always be spent immediately, no matter what
option_b: A rupee's value depends on when you receive it, and every one of these tools exists to make cash flows at different times fairly comparable
option_c: Interest rates are fixed by governments and never change
option_d: None of these concepts are related to each other
hint: What's the single thread running through every lesson in this unit?
explanation: Every tool in this unit — discounting, compounding, annuities, perpetuities, NPV, even the Rule of 72 — exists to answer one question: what is money worth, given exactly when you receive it?
